summary: Pilate tries again and again to release Jesus, but the crowd chooses Barabbas, the leaders press him, and Pilate hands Jesus over to be crucified.
key_insight: Pilate declared Jesus innocent again and again, yet he gave the sentence. What finally moved him was not evidence but a threat, recorded by John: “If you let this Man go, you are not Caesar’s friend.”
story: At the feast the governor was accustomed to releasing one prisoner whom the crowd chose. At that time there was a notorious prisoner called Barabbas, {Mt} held with the rebels who had committed murder in the rebellion. {Mk} The crowd began to ask Pilate to do as he had always done for them. {Mk}

Pilate called together the chief priests, the rulers and the people. He had examined Jesus and found no fault in Him, and neither had Herod. “I will therefore chastise Him and release Him.” {Lk} He asked, “Whom do you want me to release to you? Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?” For he knew that they had handed Him over because of envy. {Mt} While he sat on the judgment seat, his wife sent him word: “Have nothing to do with that just Man, for I have suffered many things today in a dream because of Him.” {Mt}

But the chief priests and elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas. {Mt} “Not this Man, but Barabbas!” they cried. {Jn} “What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” Pilate asked. “Let Him be crucified!” “Why, what evil has He done?” But they cried out all the more. {Mt}

Then Pilate took Jesus and scourged Him. The soldiers put a crown of thorns on His head and a purple robe on Him, and Pilate brought Him out: “Behold the Man!” When the chief priests and officers saw Him, they cried, “Crucify Him, crucify Him!” “You take Him and crucify Him,” said Pilate, “for I find no fault in Him.” The leaders answered, “We have a law, and according to our law He ought to die, because He made Himself the Son of God.” {Jn}

When Pilate heard that, he was more afraid. He went back inside and asked Jesus, “Where are You from?” Jesus gave him no answer. “Do You not know that I have power to crucify You, and power to release You?” Jesus answered, “You could have no power at all against Me unless it had been given you from above. Therefore the one who delivered Me to you has the greater sin.” {Jn}

From then on Pilate sought to release Him, but they cried out, “If you let this Man go, you are not Caesar’s friend.” So Pilate brought Jesus out and sat down in the judgment seat at the place called The Pavement, in Hebrew Gabbatha. It was the Preparation Day of the Passover, about the sixth hour. “Behold your King!” he said. “Away with Him, away with Him! Crucify Him!” “Shall I crucify your King?” The chief priests answered, “We have no king but Caesar!” {Jn}

When Pilate saw that he could not prevail and a riot was starting, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd: “I am innocent of the blood of this just Person. You see to it.” And all the people answered, “His blood be on us and on our children.” {Mt}

So Pilate, wanting to gratify the crowd, {Mk} gave sentence that it should be as they requested. He released to them the man who had been thrown into prison for rebellion and murder, and he delivered Jesus to their will {Lk} to be crucified.
differences: John places the scourging, the crown of thorns and “Behold the Man!” in the middle of the trial; Matthew and Mark mention the scourging only with the final sentence. Luke records Pilate’s offer to “chastise Him” but not the scourging itself.
Only Matthew records the message from Pilate’s wife, the washing of hands, and the cry, “His blood be on us and on our children.”
Only Luke records Pilate’s report that Herod also found nothing, and that Pilate pleaded with them “the third time.”
Only John records the second private conversation (“Where are You from?”), the charge that Jesus made Himself the Son of God, the cry about Caesar’s friend, Gabbatha and the hour.
Barabbas is “notorious” in Matthew, a rebel and murderer in Mark and Luke, and “a robber” in John.

fit.question: John places the scourging in the middle of the trial, before “Behold the Man!” Matthew and Mark mention it after the crowd’s final choice, with the sentence. When was Jesus scourged?

points.label: Mentioned with the sentence
points.text: Matthew and Mark do not tell the scourging as a scene; they mention it in passing: “when he had scourged Jesus, he delivered Him to be crucified” (Matthew 27:26). Their wording points to something already done without saying when. John shows it came earlier, as Pilate’s attempt to satisfy the crowd, which matches Luke’s “I will therefore chastise Him and release Him.”

points.label: Two beatings
points.text: Some scholars note that Romans used lighter and heavier beatings. On this view John 19:1 describes a lighter beating meant to let Jesus go, and the severe flogging that came before crucifixion followed the sentence.

fit.note: Each writer reports a scourging, and none says it happened only at the point where he mentions it. Either explanation fits the texts.
fit.short: Matthew and Mark mention the scourging with the sentence; John shows when it happened. Or there were two beatings, a lighter and a heavier.

scene.label: The Passover release
scene.text: The Gospels are our only record of this custom. Roman governors could pardon prisoners, and a release at the feast that celebrated Israel’s freedom from Egypt would have been a popular gesture.

scene.label: Barabbas
scene.text: His name is Aramaic for son of the father. He was a rebel against Rome and a killer, the very kind of man the leaders claimed Jesus was. John’s word “robber” was also used in that day for violent rebels.

scene.label: Roman scourging
scene.text: Roman flogging used a whip of leather straps weighted with bits of bone or metal. It tore the back open, and some prisoners died under it. The Jewish limit of forty lashes (Deuteronomy 25:3) did not bind Roman soldiers.

scene.label: “Caesar’s friend”
scene.text: The title friend of Caesar was an honor given to loyal officials. Emperor Tiberius was quick to suspect disloyalty, and treason charges ruined many careers. A report that Pilate had freed a man who claimed to be a king could have cost him his post.

scene.label: Washing hands
scene.text: The Law told the elders of a town to wash their hands over a heifer when an unsolved murder was found and to say, “Our hands have not shed this blood” (Deuteronomy 21:6–7). Pilate may have known the custom, or simply used a gesture everyone understood.

witnesses.matthew: Gathers voices that call Jesus innocent: Pilate’s wife (“that just Man”), Pilate himself (“this just Person”), coming right after Judas’s “innocent blood.” The people’s cry, “His blood be on us and on our children,” was later misused to blame the Jewish people as a whole; Matthew himself records that Jesus’ blood was “shed for many for the remission of sins” (26:28).
witnesses.mark: Puts it plainly: Pilate knew the chief priests acted out of envy, yet “wanting to gratify the crowd” he gave in. The rebel and murderer walks free, and the innocent Man is handed over.
witnesses.luke: Records Pilate saying three times that Jesus had done nothing deserving death, and adds Herod’s agreement. His phrase “delivered Jesus to their will” shows a judge who surrendered justice to a crowd.
witnesses.john: Builds the trial to its climax with Pilate’s two announcements, “Behold the Man!” and “Behold your King!” Only John records the second private conversation, where Jesus tells Pilate his power was given from above, and the chief priests’ final words: “We have no king but Caesar!”

seeing.reveals: Jesus, scourged and crowned with thorns, tells Pilate that his power is only what God has given him. The innocent One is condemned, and the guilty Barabbas walks free in His place.
seeing.living: Barabbas went free because Jesus was condemned; that is what Jesus’ death means for every sinner who trusts Him. Pilate tried every way to avoid deciding about Jesus, and every way failed. No one can wash their hands of Him.
seeing.ponder: Pilate asked, “What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” What is your answer?

preaching.big_idea: Everyone at Pilate’s judgment seat made a choice about Jesus; no one could stay neutral.
preaching.watch_for: John frames the scene with Pilate’s two announcements, “Behold the Man!” (19:5) and “Behold your King!” (19:14). It ends with the chief priests choosing Caesar over the King God sent (19:15).
